title: A disallowed goal and a red card awarded with the conviction of Inspector Clouseau. Just scrap VAR
content:
Craig Pawson is the referee and he is rolling chewing gum around his mouth like a New York City cop who thinks he has the crime scene under control. Except, as he begins to try to explain away some of the grisly details, the gum rests awkwardly on his tongue and interferes with his speech.

For anyone listening inside the stadium or at home on television, the audio is so bad that Pawson might as well be broadcasting his findings from underneath a fallen tree in a Siberian forest. This is not the drama it could be; say, if a voice boomed out like God across Anfield’s public address system, striking thunder onto the pitch.

Instead, Pawson works backwards with the conviction of Inspector Jacques Clouseau.

If you replay the moment, you find out what he actually said: “After review, there is a careless foul by Erling Haaland that pulls the shirt of Dominik Szoboszlai. Prior to that, Szoboszlai commits a holding offence that denies an obvious goalscoring opportunity. The final decision is a direct free kick to Manchester City and a red card (for Szoboszlai).”

It means City beat Liverpool by two goals to one rather than three, even though Haaland would not have been in a position to foul Szoboszlai had the Hungarian not pulled him back as he chased down towards an unguarded net, attempting to catch up with the most ridiculous, piddling shot from the halfway line you have ever seen.

All of this happened while the officials at distant Stockley Park were actually conducting a separate VAR check for a penalty at the other end of the pitch following claims of a foul on Federico Chiesa. Welcome to the chaos.

Desperation had driven Liverpool to this.

With goalkeeper Alisson masquerading as Peter Crouch upfield in Liverpool’s attack, Szoboszlai aimed his delivery roughly in his direction from deep, but City’s Marc Guehi won the first header. Bernardo Silva hooked a short clearance to Rayan Cherki, who, from just inside his own half and with the goal unprotected at the far end, released a shot of which an anaemic crane fly would have been proud.

This, on reflection, was probably the most significant cause of the events that followed. It made Haaland think there was still work to do to nudge the ball across the line, and it made Szoboszlai believe he had a chance of stopping him.

The funniest bit was Szoboszlai trying to convince Pawson that he had been fouled before the referee went to the monitor. Szoboszlai had been fouled, of course, but only because his own actions had created that possibility.

His night had already been eventful, having planted a wonderful free kick past Gianluigi Donnarumma in front of the Kop to give Liverpool the lead, before reminding those present why — despite his clear talent — his game might not yet be where it could be. He played a role in City’s equaliser, switching off at the far post and playing Silva onside.

In the heat of Anfield, maybe Szoboszlai forgot that modern football grounds rival the most heavily policed nations when it comes to cameras. When you tug on the shirt of a massive centre-forward with a blond ponytail who is hurtling towards his intended destination like a bus with no brakes, it gets picked up straight away.

The City players celebrated with their fans, knowing victory kept them in a title race with Arsenal, only for Pawson to be sent to his monitor by the VAR assistant John Brooks.

Admittedly, I feel a bit sorry for Pawson — especially in this situation because he is only doing his job. He is following orders, and someone ultimately has to front it unless we cede entirely to bots and/or bureaucratic types who make sweeping decisions from their desks hundreds of miles away.

Yet when you watch an official like Pawson browsing the screen — and he always does this with his hands on his hips — you are immediately taken to the parking bay when your car is literally inches just over the line but the attendant doesn’t care.

Rules are rules, photographic evidence is being taken, and you, sir, are going in the book.

Gary Neville spoke first on the matter, as he tends to, with the pundit saying on Sky Sports, “No football person would disallow that goal.” On this occasion, I agree with him.

The cold, common-sense decision would be a goal for City and maybe a card of some kind for Szoboszlai. He clearly deserves some punishment, but nothing that would stop his opponents from being awarded their third goal. Before the VAR system, it would certainly have stood and nobody would have complained. Rather, there would have been an acceptance that Szoboszlai and Haaland both fouled each other before the ball rolled across the line.

Instead, the VAR has ended up denying a goal to punish a player who unsuccessfully tried to stop a goal.

By the letter of the current weird law, yes, the officials got it right, but the law is a problem here because Haaland’s reaction should surely not define how the sequence is viewed.

I’m exhausted by the VAR system and I’m fed up with being asked to discuss its place in football. There is too much stop-starting, too many rule changes, which means I often don’t know what is real anymore. Too many times it has made me check whether it’s safe to enjoy myself before someone, who could probably sit there in his undies if he wanted to, eating crisps all day, changes everything because of the interference of a stray pubic hair.

Total abolition is preferable. Enough.
